description: Innovators, builders, and problem solvers. We transform complex challenges into real-world prototypes using code, design, and plenty of creativity.
summary:
FireCal is a web application featuring a harmonized calendar of fire activity for Cochabamba, Bolivia, covering the period from 2000 to the present. MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) satellites record fire hotspots in very different ways; for instance, in October 2026, VIIRS recorded more than three times as many detections in Bolivia as MODIS did. Simply combining these datasets without adjustment would create the false impression that fire activity had increased, when in fact only the instrument had changed.
We calculated a monthly conversion factor to align 26 years of MODIS data with the VIIRS scale, ensuring that data from the two sensors are never simply added together. When tested against years not included in the model’s training, we achieved a correlation of 0.987.
Users can select a specific area to view peak activity months, compare the current month against its historical median, and identify the types of vegetation being burned. For the Cercado municipality, integration with the local government’s API allows for a detailed breakdown by district.
This provides the regional government (Gobernación), the national protected areas service (SERNAP), and volunteers with a reliable answer to a critical question: is this month normal or not?
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

FireCal is a web application with a harmonized fire activity calendar for the department of Cochabamba, Bolivia, from 2000 to the present. It uses heat hotspot detections from NASA FIRMS, drawing on three sources: MODIS (1 km, since 2000), VIIRS S-NPP (375 m, since 2012) and VIIRS NOAA-20.

Because the sensors count fire very differently, we first apply the recommended quality filters: minimum confidence and vegetation-fire sources only. Then we calculate a conversion factor for each month of the year, using the period when both sensors were operating together. This way, the entire series is expressed in “VIIRS S-NPP equivalent.” We never add up two sensors for the same period. When S-NPP stopped sending data in November 2026, the system automatically switched to NOAA-20, with its own factor. We validated the method by calibrating with 2012–2018 and testing with 2019–2026: the correlation was 0.987 and the error was 4.7 times lower than using uncorrected MODIS.

Users choose one of the critical zones, delimited using the real municipal boundaries: Tunari, Trópico, TIPNIS/Carrasco, Cono Sur and others. They can also draw their own area. The application shows:

  • the months and years with the most activity;
  • the current month compared with its historical median;
  • which vegetation burns in that zone;
  • a 3D map of hotspots and a ranking by municipality.

In the municipality of Cercado, we connect to the WMS API of the Cochabamba Municipal Government (Alcaldía). This lets us label each hotspot with its district, whether it lies above the 2,750 m contour (the protection limit of Tunari Park), and its peri-urban zone, and we obtain a ranking by district. The official hectares from the Departmental Government (Gobernación) and SERNAP are displayed alongside as validation, without being mixed with the detections. Everything can be downloaded as CSV, PDF or Excel.

Expected benefits and impact

Today, anyone comparing data from different years or satellites may conclude that fire has tripled when only the instrument changed. FireCal gives the Departmental Risk Management Unit (UGR) of the Gobernación, the municipalities, SERNAP, firefighters and volunteers such as Tunari Sin Fuego a comparable 26-year series. With it, they can answer a key question for planning patrols and prevention campaigns: is this month normal or not? For example, in the first half of November 2026, the Trópico had already doubled the median of a full November. The method can be applied to any region of the world with FIRMS data.

Tools used

  • Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS S-NPP and NOAA-20), Bolivian municipal boundaries, and the WMS API of the Cochabamba Municipal Government (GAMC).
  • Processing: Python 3, pandas and shapely.
  • Server (API): Node.js 20 and Express, deployed on Railway.
  • Web page: React, Vite, Leaflet and deck.gl (3D map), published on Firebase Hosting.
  • Collaboration: Git and GitHub, with an MVC architecture split among the three team members.

What is creative about it?

  • A calendar instead of a point map: it turns 26 years of data into something anyone can understand at a glance.
  • Integration with the Municipal Government: it combines global satellite data with municipal data down to the district level.
  • Vegetation by zone: each zone shows what is burning (eucalyptus, pine, grassland, kewiña, humid forest) to give context to the numbers.
  • Languages: the interface is in Spanish and English, with a preliminary Quechua version.

Factors we took into account

  • Scientific rigor: a detection is a hot pixel, not a fire, so we say “hotspots” and not “fires”; we do not add sensors together; we do not present anything as a prediction.
  • Transparency: official figures are shown alongside, never mixed in.
  • Accessibility: colorblind-friendly palettes (viridis and PuOr).
  • Security: API keys never reach the browser or GitHub.
  • Respect for the municipal API: queries are sent one at a time, with pauses and local caching, so as not to overload it.
  • Real users: we designed around what the UGR, SERNAP and volunteers actually need.
